scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document (title, methods, results, and discussion) concerns a computational phenotyping algorithm for identifying post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC/long COVID) using Massachusetts EHR data; Lyme disease is never mentioned in the document's own text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This peer-reviewed study (Azhir et al., 2025, Med) developed a computer algorithm to more accurately identify patients with long COVID (PASC) from electronic health records, comparing it to the standard U09.9 diagnosis code. Using data from over 295,000 patients across 14 hospitals and 20 community health centers in Massachusetts, the algorithm identified 24,360 long-haulers with 79.9% precision, versus 77.8% precision for the U09.9 code alone, and produced a less demographically biased cohort. The study reports how common different organ-system symptom clusters were among COVID-19 patients and documents that the U09.9 code undercounts and skews whom it identifies (toward White, female patients). It does not report any dollar costs, insurance/access burden, lost income, or caregiving time - its contribution is to diagnostic/phenotyping accuracy and demographic bias in identifying long COVID cases, not economic burden.

contextual_issues: The paper describes PASC as requiring a 'diagnosis of exclusion' process that distinguishes new symptoms from pre-existing conditions, implying repeated clinical encounters and diagnostic work-up, but does not quantify visits, time-to-diagnosis, or care-seeking burden.

The paper notes that having a prior PASC increases the chance of developing more PASC after a subsequent infection, suggesting cumulative illness burden across repeat infections, but gives no quantified odds ratio or burden measure for this specific claim.
Declining frequency of COVID-19 testing over time is mentioned as a limitation for applying the algorithm (a data/surveillance access issue), not a patient-facing access barrier.

Rare but notable symptoms (sexual dysfunction/low libido, vision/hearing loss, gynecological complications) are described qualitatively as organ-system findings without further burden quantification beyond the stated organ-level counts already captured above.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost data (e.g., visit, hospitalization, medication costs) are reported anywhere in the document for either PASC or Lyme disease.
No direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help) or indirect costs (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time) are reported.
No insurance coverage, access-barrier, or affordability data are reported.

The cohort is followed for only 12 months after last infection, so no data exist in this document to support lifetime or multi-year cost/burden projections without an added, clearly labeled extrapolation assumption.
Lyme disease is not addressed anywhere in this document; no Lyme-specific case counts, cost, or burden data can be drawn from it.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the algorithm's raw/adjusted EHR-derived prevalence estimates (28.5%/22.8%, MGB cohort, COVID-19 cases 03/2020-06/2023 with 12-month follow-up) with the cited NCHS Household Pulse Survey estimate (24.0%, Massachusetts, June 1 2022-Oct 2 2023) - these differ in data source (computational EHR phenotyping vs. self-reported household survey), population definition, and measurement time window, even though they are presented side by side as a validation comparison.

Do not pool the U09.9-based raw case count (6,340 patients, and the PPV-adjusted 'under 5,000' estimate) with the algorithm-based long-hauler count (24,360 patients) as if they were two confidence levels of the same measurement - they use different case-identification methods (single ICD-10 code vs. diagnosis-of-exclusion algorithm) applied to data with different inclusion criteria.

Organ-system burden figures are reported against two different denominators - percentage of all COVID-19 cases (n=85,364) versus percentage of algorithm-identified long-haulers (n=24,360) - and must not be added or compared without specifying which denominator is used.

Post-pandemic controls (matched 1:2 on sex/race/age/Charlson score, n=170,497, dates 2017-2023) and pre-pandemic controls (unmatched, smaller, n=39,817, dates 2015-2020) are structurally different comparison groups and must not be pooled into a single control estimate.

sex_gender_findings.finding: After adjusting for demographics and comorbidities, women had significantly higher odds of developing systemic, GI, neurological, skin, mental-health-related, musculoskeletal, and gynecological PASC than men (odds ratios in Table S4; 95% CIs in Figure 5). Odds of respiratory, renal/genitourinary, endocrine, and eyes-and-ears PASC were not significantly different between sexes at the study's p<0.05 threshold. Separately, in the raw demographic counts, 64.5% of algorithm-identified long-haulers were female versus 62.6% of the overall COVID-19 case cohort, and 67.5% of U09.9-coded patients were female versus 51% of the Massachusetts general population (cited from US Census).

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The document's own modeled values for U09.9-based PASC counts (6,340 raw U09.9-coded patients; the PPV-adjusted 'under 5,000' estimate) are explicitly drawn from an ICD-10 diagnosis-code (U09.9) basis in the MGB EHR, which the document itself states 'lacks sensitivity and specificity' and showed demographic skew. In addition, the algorithm's own prevalence estimates (28.5% raw / 22.8% adjusted) are derived from structured EHR diagnosis/procedure codes (CCSR categories built from ICD-10-CM/PCS codes), and the Limitations section explicitly states 'our reliance on structured data may have resulted in an underestimation of PASC.'

scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This peer-reviewed study (Azhir et al., 2025, Med) developed a computer algorithm to more accurately identify patients with long COVID (PASC) from electronic health records, comparing it to the standard U09.9 diagnosis code. Using data from over 295,000 patients across 14 hospitals and 20 community health centers in Massachusetts, the algorithm identified 24,360 long-haulers with 79.9% precision, versus 77.8% precision for the U09.9 code alone, and produced a less demographically biased cohort. The study reports how common different organ-system symptom clusters were among COVID-19 patients and documents that the U09.9 code undercounts and skews whom it identifies (toward White, female patients). It does not report any dollar costs, insurance/access burden, lost income, or caregiving time - its contribution is to diagnostic/phenotyping accuracy and demographic bias in identifying long COVID cases, not economic burden.

Declining frequency of COVID-19 testing over time is mentioned as a limitation for applying the algorithm (a data/surveillance access issue), not a patient-facing access barrier.

spec.title: Long COVID Case-Identification: Algorithm vs. U09.9 Diagnosis Code (Azhir et al. 2025)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces precision, prevalence, demographic-composition, and organ-system-symptom figures from a single peer-reviewed study (Azhir et al., 2025, Med) comparing a computational phenotyping algorithm against the U09.9 ICD-10 diagnosis code for identifying long COVID (PASC) in Mass General Brigham electronic health record data (14 hospitals, 20 community health centers), for COVID-19 infections from March 2020-June 2023 with 12-month follow-up. It does not include any dollar cost, insurance/access, lost-income, or caregiving-burden data, because the source document reports none of these. It does not address Lyme disease at all, since the uploaded document's entire subject is long COVID diagnostic/phenotyping methodology.

takeaway.patient: A research study compared two ways of counting long COVID patients in health records: relying on a single official diagnosis code (U09.9) versus a more thorough computer-based review of symptoms. The computer-based approach found more patients overall, and found a patient group that was less skewed toward White patients than the group found by the single code alone. This suggests that counts based only on the official diagnosis code may miss people with real long COVID symptoms, especially from under-represented groups, and are not a complete picture of who has long COVID.
takeaway.care: Within this one health system, relying solely on the U09.9 diagnosis code to identify long COVID patients produced a smaller, more demographically skewed (more White, more female) group of confirmed cases than a structured computational phenotyping approach did; the code also had slightly lower confirmed precision (77.8%) than the algorithm (79.9%) on chart review. Among algorithm-identified long-haulers, systemic symptoms (fatigue, pain, sleep, weight/nutrition changes) were the most common cluster (about 41% of long-haulers in this cohort).
takeaway.policy: Official ICD-10 code-based surveillance (U09.9) in this Massachusetts health-system dataset undercounted confirmed long COVID cases relative to a validated computational phenotyping algorithm, and skewed the captured population toward White and female patients. The study's authors also note that, as of publication, no scalable, universally accepted phenotyping method or diagnosis code existed for long COVID, which they state has hindered enrollment in large-scale treatment trials.

patient: If you have lingering symptoms after a COVID-19 infection but have never been given the U09.9 long COVID code, understand that this study suggests code-based counts can miss patients like you - this may be worth raising with your clinician as a question about whether your symptoms fit a long COVID pattern, even without that specific code on your chart.

If you are comparing long COVID prevalence numbers you see in the news (for example, 22.8% from this algorithm-based study versus 24.0% from a separate self-reported survey), know these come from different methods, populations, and time windows and are not directly interchangeable - treat differing numbers as reflecting different measurement approaches, not as one being simply wrong.

If you experience fatigue, gastrointestinal, neurological, skin, mental-health, or musculoskeletal symptoms after COVID, this study found women had significantly higher odds of these specific symptom types than men did (while odds for respiratory, kidney/urinary, hormone-related, or eye/ear symptoms did not differ significantly by sex in this study) - this may be a useful pattern to mention to your own clinician when describing your symptoms.
care: This finding - that relying only on the U09.9 code produced a smaller and more demographically skewed (more White, more female) group than a structured phenotyping approach - may be worth checking against your own site's registry or referral criteria for long COVID patients.

Consider whether intake or follow-up screening for post-COVID symptoms systematically covers the organ-system clusters found most common in this cohort (systemic symptoms in roughly 41% of long-haulers, gastrointestinal in roughly 16%), to help with specialty referral capacity planning.

Note that women had significantly higher odds of systemic, gastrointestinal, neurological, skin, mental-health, and musculoskeletal PASC than men in this study, while respiratory, renal/genitourinary, endocrine, and eye/ear PASC odds did not differ significantly by sex - this distinction may be worth building into symptom-screening checklists rather than treating all organ systems as equally sex-differentiated.

For research cohort development, this result suggests a structured phenotyping approach, rather than a single diagnosis code, may be worth evaluating as a supplement for identifying a more representative long COVID patient population for studies or quality programs.
policy: Agencies or health systems overseeing long COVID surveillance could evaluate whether reliance on U09.9 coding alone understates caseload and skews demographic representation in registries, using this study's method as one illustrative comparison.

Research funders or health systems could consider supporting broader validation and adoption of computational phenotyping approaches to improve equity in long COVID research cohort composition and clinical trial enrollment, consistent with the study authors' observation that the absence of a robust phenotyping method had hindered large-scale trial enrollment.

When citing long COVID prevalence figures in policy documents, specify the measurement method, population, and time window (for example, this algorithm-based estimate for a Massachusetts health system during 2020-2023 versus a separately cited self-reported national survey estimate for Massachusetts during 2022-2023) rather than treating differing figures as directly comparable or interchangeable.

This simulator reproduces figures from Azhir et al. (2025, Med), a peer-reviewed study comparing a computational phenotyping algorithm against the U09.9 ICD-10 diagnosis code for identifying long COVID (PASC) in Mass General Brigham (MGB) electronic health records (14 hospitals, 20 community health centers), for COVID-19 infections from March 2020-June 2023 with 12-month follow-up.

**Inputs** reproduce the study's own reported chart-review-validated precision (PPV) for the algorithm (79.9%) and the U09.9 code (77.8%), the raw algorithm-flagged prevalence (28.5% of COVID-19 cases), the raw U09.9-coded patient count (6,340), the algorithm-identified long-hauler count (24,360), each cohort's White-patient share (71.4% algorithm vs. 80.1% U09.9), and the share of long-haulers with systemic-category symptoms (41.2%).

**Outputs** recompute: (1) the PPV-adjusted algorithm prevalence, which the document itself also reports as approximately 22.8% - this recomputation may differ slightly from the document's own figure due to rounding; (2) a PPV-adjusted estimate of confirmed PASC patients within the U09.9-coded cohort, approximating the document's stated "under 5,000" figure; (3) the gap between the algorithm-identified count and this adjusted U09.9 estimate, labeled so the sign is explicit; (4) the gap in White-patient share between the two identification methods; (5) the number of algorithm-identified long-haulers with systemic symptoms.

**Limitations.** Both the U09.9-code-based counts and the algorithm's own prevalence estimates rely on structured ICD-10/EHR diagnosis and procedure codes; the authors state this reliance on structured data "may have resulted in an underestimation of PASC," so neither figure should be read as a complete count of long COVID burden. The overall prevalence estimates (28.5%/22.8%) are reported as single pooled figures without breakdown by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; only organ-system-specific PASC odds (not the overall prevalence rate) were broken down this way. On sex: after adjustment, women had significantly higher odds of systemic, gastrointestinal, neurological, skin, mental-health, and musculoskeletal PASC than men, while odds of respiratory, renal/genitourinary, endocrine, and eyes/ears PASC did not differ significantly by sex at the study's threshold. Federal survey data (MEPS, NHIS, BRFSS) generally supports disaggregated analysis by sex, age, and race/ethnicity even though this document did not perform it for the overall prevalence figures. Separately, the study describes a measurement-infrastructure gap: as of publication, no scalable, universally accepted phenotyping algorithm or diagnosis code existed for identifying PASC, which the authors state "hindered effective enrollment for large-scale clinical studies of potential therapies." This document reports no dollar costs, insurance/access data, lost income, or caregiving burden, and does not address Lyme disease; no economic-burden outputs are included here.

spec.title: Long COVID Case-Identification: Algorithm vs. U09.9 Diagnosis Code (Azhir et al. 2025)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces precision, prevalence, demographic-composition, and organ-system-symptom figures from a single peer-reviewed study (Azhir et al., 2025, Med) comparing a computational phenotyping algorithm against the U09.9 ICD-10 diagnosis code for identifying long COVID (PASC) in Mass General Brigham electronic health record data (14 hospitals, 20 community health centers), for COVID-19 infections from March 2020-June 2023 with 12-month follow-up. It does not include any dollar cost, insurance/access, lost-income, or caregiving-burden data, because the source document reports none of these. It does not address Lyme disease at all, since the uploaded document's entire subject is long COVID diagnostic/phenotyping methodology.

takeaway.patient: A research study compared two ways of counting long COVID patients in health records: relying on a single official diagnosis code (U09.9) versus a more thorough computer-based review of symptoms. The computer-based approach found more patients overall, and found a patient group that was less skewed toward White patients than the group found by the single code alone. This suggests that counts based only on the official diagnosis code may miss people with real long COVID symptoms, especially from under-represented groups, and are not a complete picture of who has long COVID.
takeaway.care: Within this one health system, relying solely on the U09.9 diagnosis code to identify long COVID patients produced a smaller, more demographically skewed (more White, more female) group of confirmed cases than a structured computational phenotyping approach did; the code also had slightly lower confirmed precision (77.8%) than the algorithm (79.9%) on chart review. Among algorithm-identified long-haulers, systemic symptoms (fatigue, pain, sleep, weight/nutrition changes) were the most common cluster (about 41% of long-haulers in this cohort).
takeaway.policy: Official ICD-10 code-based surveillance (U09.9) in this Massachusetts health-system dataset undercounted confirmed long COVID cases relative to a validated computational phenotyping algorithm, and skewed the captured population toward White and female patients. The study's authors also note that, as of publication, no scalable, universally accepted phenotyping method or diagnosis code existed for long COVID, which they state has hindered enrollment in large-scale treatment trials.

patient: If you have lingering symptoms after a COVID-19 infection but have never been given the U09.9 long COVID code, understand that this study suggests code-based counts can miss patients like you - this may be worth raising with your clinician as a question about whether your symptoms fit a long COVID pattern, even without that specific code on your chart.

If you are comparing long COVID prevalence numbers you see in the news (for example, 22.8% from this algorithm-based study versus 24.0% from a separate self-reported survey), know these come from different methods, populations, and time windows and are not directly interchangeable - treat differing numbers as reflecting different measurement approaches, not as one being simply wrong.

If you experience fatigue, gastrointestinal, neurological, skin, mental-health, or musculoskeletal symptoms after COVID, this study found women had significantly higher odds of these specific symptom types than men did (while odds for respiratory, kidney/urinary, hormone-related, or eye/ear symptoms did not differ significantly by sex in this study) - this may be a useful pattern to mention to your own clinician when describing your symptoms.
care: This finding - that relying only on the U09.9 code produced a smaller and more demographically skewed (more White, more female) group than a structured phenotyping approach - may be worth checking against your own site's registry or referral criteria for long COVID patients.

Consider whether intake or follow-up screening for post-COVID symptoms systematically covers the organ-system clusters found most common in this cohort (systemic symptoms in roughly 41% of long-haulers, gastrointestinal in roughly 16%), to help with specialty referral capacity planning.

Note that women had significantly higher odds of systemic, gastrointestinal, neurological, skin, mental-health, and musculoskeletal PASC than men in this study, while respiratory, renal/genitourinary, endocrine, and eye/ear PASC odds did not differ significantly by sex - this distinction may be worth building into symptom-screening checklists rather than treating all organ systems as equally sex-differentiated.

For research cohort development, this result suggests a structured phenotyping approach, rather than a single diagnosis code, may be worth evaluating as a supplement for identifying a more representative long COVID patient population for studies or quality programs.
policy: Agencies or health systems overseeing long COVID surveillance could evaluate whether reliance on U09.9 coding alone understates caseload and skews demographic representation in registries, using this study's method as one illustrative comparison.

Research funders or health systems could consider supporting broader validation and adoption of computational phenotyping approaches to improve equity in long COVID research cohort composition and clinical trial enrollment, consistent with the study authors' observation that the absence of a robust phenotyping method had hindered large-scale trial enrollment.

When citing long COVID prevalence figures in policy documents, specify the measurement method, population, and time window (for example, this algorithm-based estimate for a Massachusetts health system during 2020-2023 versus a separately cited self-reported national survey estimate for Massachusetts during 2022-2023) rather than treating differing figures as directly comparable or interchangeable.

inputs.label: Raw algorithm-flagged PASC prevalence
inputs.source: Azhir et al. 2025, Med, Results/Discussion, p.3; 15.0-40.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own reported share of COVID-19 cases flagged as having at least one PASC symptom cluster by the phenotyping algorithm, before correcting for precision; moving it tests how sensitive the PPV-adjusted prevalence output is to this starting detection rate.

inputs.label: Algorithm precision (PPV)
inputs.source: Azhir et al. 2025, Med, Results, p.3; 60.0-95.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the algorithm's chart-review-validated precision: the share of algorithm-flagged patients confirmed to truly have PASC on manual review. Raising or lowering it shows how much the PPV-adjusted prevalence depends on how reliable the algorithm's flags are.

inputs.label: U09.9-coded patient count
inputs.source: Azhir et al. 2025, Med, Results, p.3; 3000-10000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the total number of MGB patients who received the U09.9 long COVID diagnosis code during the study period; moving it shows how the adjusted true-PASC estimate for code-based identification would change if raw code usage were higher or lower.

inputs.label: U09.9 code precision (PPV)
inputs.source: Azhir et al. 2025, Med, Results, p.3; 60.0-95.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the U09.9 code's own chart-review-validated precision; a lower value means a larger share of coded patients did not actually have confirmed PASC on review, which drives the gap against the algorithm-identified count.

inputs.label: Algorithm-identified long-hauler count
inputs.source: Azhir et al. 2025, Med, Results, p.3; 15000-35000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's own reported count of patients the phenotyping algorithm identified as long-haulers; it anchors both the count-difference and systemic-symptom-count outputs below.

inputs.label: White-patient share, algorithm-identified cohort
inputs.source: Azhir et al. 2025, Med, Results, p.3; 50.0-90.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the White-patient share of the algorithm-identified long-hauler cohort reported by the document; comparing it against the U09.9 cohort's share tests how much the identification method itself affects demographic representativeness.

inputs.label: White-patient share, U09.9-coded cohort
inputs.source: Azhir et al. 2025, Med, Results, p.3; 50.0-90.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the White-patient share of the U09.9-coded cohort reported by the document; the study found this share was higher than the algorithm-identified cohort's, consistent with code-based identification skewing toward White patients.

inputs.label: Systemic-symptom share among long-haulers
inputs.source: Azhir et al. 2025, Med, Results, p.3; 20.0-60.0 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported share of algorithm-identified long-haulers with systemic-category symptoms (edema, generalized pain, sleep disorders, fatigue, etc.); moving it rescales the systemic-symptom patient count, useful for specialty capacity planning.

outputs.label: PPV-adjusted algorithm PASC prevalence
outputs.interpretation: This multiplies the raw algorithm-flagged prevalence (28.5%) by the algorithm's own validated precision (79.9%) to estimate the share of true-positive PASC cases. The document itself also reports this adjusted estimate as approximately 22.8%; this recomputation may differ very slightly from that stated figure due to rounding. A higher value means more confidence that the raw flag rate reflects true PASC rather than false positives.

outputs.label: PPV-adjusted true-PASC estimate within U09.9-coded cohort
outputs.interpretation: This applies the U09.9 code's own chart-review-validated precision (77.8%) to the raw count of 6,340 U09.9-coded patients, approximating the document's own statement that under 5,000 of these patients likely had confirmed PASC. A lower value means a larger share of U09.9-coded patients were false positives (coded without confirmed PASC on review).

outputs.label: Algorithm-identified count minus PPV-adjusted U09.9 estimate (positive = algorithm identifies more confirmed patients; negative = U09.9 approach identifies more)
outputs.interpretation: A positive value means the computational phenotyping algorithm identified more confirmed long COVID patients than the single-code approach captured in this same health system and period; a negative value would mean the opposite. These two counts come from different identification methods (a diagnosis-of-exclusion algorithm vs. a single ICD-10 code measuring billed diagnoses), so this gap reflects a difference in measurement approach, not one correcting the other - which figure is more relevant depends on whether the decision at hand needs a sensitive research-cohort definition or a narrower, currently billable diagnosis.

outputs.label: White-patient share, algorithm cohort minus U09.9 cohort (negative = algorithm identifies a less White-skewed group; positive = algorithm identifies a more White-skewed group)
outputs.interpretation: A negative value (as in the document's own reported figures) means the algorithm identified a less White-skewed group of long COVID patients than relying on the U09.9 code alone, consistent with the study's finding that code-based identification skewed toward White, female patients. A positive value would mean the opposite pattern.

outputs.label: Algorithm-identified long-haulers with systemic symptoms
outputs.interpretation: This multiplies the algorithm-identified long-hauler count by the systemic-symptom share to approximate the document's own reported count of about 10,044 such patients; the recomputed value may differ very slightly due to rounding in the reported percentage. A higher value indicates systemic symptoms (fatigue, pain, sleep, weight/nutrition changes) make up a larger share of the overall long COVID symptom burden in this cohort.
